## Problem 1

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)

data("ny_noaa")

# Check data shape and structure
dim(ny_noaa)
glimpse(ny_noaa)
```

```{r}
# Check NA proportion of each variable
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "proportion_missing"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion_missing))
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. Each row represents a daily weather observation from a NOAA weather station in New York State. Key variables include station ID (`id`), date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`). The `date` variable is stored as a date, while `prcp`, `snow`, and `snwd` are stored as integers; `tmax` and `tmin` are currently stored as character variables and will require cleaning before analysis.

Missing data are a substantial issue in this dataset. Approximately 43.7% of observations are missing for both `tmin` and `tmax`, while 22.8% are missing for `snwd`, 14.7% for `snow`, and 5.6% for `prcp`. The station ID and date variables have no missing values.

```{r}
# Clean the NY NOAA data and create separate date variables
ny_noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    # Extract year, month, and day from the date variable
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),

    # Convert temperature variables to degrees Celsius
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,

    # Convert precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth to millimeters
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    snow = snow / 10,
    snwd = snwd / 10
  )

# Check the structure of the cleaned dataset
glimpse(ny_noaa_clean)
```

I first cleaned the dataset by separating the date into year, month, and day variables and converting the weather measurements into more interpretable units.

```{r}
# Summarize the cleaned weather variables
ny_noaa_clean |>
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp, snow, snwd) |>
  summary()
```

```{r}
# Identify the most commonly observed snowfall values
ny_noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. This is expected because snowfall occurs only on a relatively small number of days, so zero snowfall is much more common than any positive amount. Among nonzero values, small snowfall amounts such as 2.5 mm, 1.3 mm, and 5.1 mm are observed relatively frequently, which is consistent with light snowfall events being more common than heavy snowfall.

```{r}
# Calculate average maximum temperature in January and July

jan_jul_temp =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax))

# Label the month
jan_jul_temp =
  jan_jul_temp |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

# Plot average maximum temperature by station across years
ggplot(
  jan_jul_temp,
  aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average January and July Maximum Temperatures by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Average maximum temperatures are substantially lower and more variable in January than in July. January station-level averages are generally centered near 0°C, while July averages are mostly in the mid-to-upper 20s °C. There is substantial year-to-year variation, especially in January, but no strong monotonic temporal trend is immediately apparent. A few unusually low station-year averages appear in both months and may represent outliers or stations with unusual local conditions.

```{r}
# Plot the joint distribution of maximum and minimum temperatures
temp_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    !is.na(tmax),
    !is.na(tmin)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "blue1",
    high = "blue4"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Keep positive snowfall values below 100 mm and summarize snowfall distributions within each year
snow_plot_data =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) |>
  mutate(
    snow_bin = floor(snow / 5) * 5
  ) |>
  count(year, snow_bin) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Plot snowfall distributions separately by year
snow_plot =
  snow_plot_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = snow_bin,
      y = factor(year),
      fill = proportion
    )
  ) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "skyblue1",
    high = "skyblue4"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm; 5-mm bins)",
    y = "Year",
    fill = "Within-year proportion"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=15}
# Create two-panel plot
library(patchwork)
temp_plot / snow_plot
```

Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship, with most observations concentrated along an upward-sloping band. Most daily maximum temperatures are higher than the corresponding minimum temperatures, as expected. A small number of extreme observations appear far from the main distribution and may reflect unusual or erroneous measurements.

Across years, positive snowfall amounts below 100 mm are concentrated in the smaller snowfall bins, while larger snowfall amounts occur much less frequently. This pattern is fairly consistent across years, although some year-to-year variation is present.


## Problem 2

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Load demographic data
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4
  )

# Load accelerometer data
nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
```

```{r}
# Check dimensions and variable structure
dim(nhanes_covar)
glimpse(nhanes_covar)

# Check accelerometer dimensions and selected variables
dim(nhanes_accel)

nhanes_accel |>
  select(SEQN, min1:min5, min1436:min1440) |>
  glimpse()
```

```{r}
# Tidy accelerometer data into long format
nhanes_accel_tidy =
  nhanes_accel |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(str_remove(minute, "min"))
  )
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_clean =
  nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r}
# Check the cleaned and merged data
dim(nhanes_covar_clean)

nhanes_data |>
  select(SEQN, minute, MIMS, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
dim(nhanes_data)
```

```{r}
n_distinct(nhanes_data$SEQN)
```

After excluding participants younger than 21 years and those with missing demographic information, 228 participants remained. The accelerometer data were converted to long format with one observation per participant-minute, resulting in 328,320 observations.

```{r}
# Count participants by education level and sex
education_sex_table =
  nhanes_covar_clean |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )

# Create a reader-friendly table
education_sex_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Education level", "Male", "Female"),
    caption = "Number of Participants by Education Level and Sex"
  )
```

The largest education category is "More than high school," with similar numbers of men and women. The "High school equivalent" group contains more men than women, while the "Less than high school" group is approximately balanced by sex.

```{r}
# Plot age distributions by sex and education level
ggplot(
  nhanes_covar_clean,
  aes(
    x = age,
    fill = sex,
    color = sex
  )
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Age distributions differ across education categories. Participants with more than a high school education tend to be younger, whereas those with less than a high school education are more concentrated at older ages. Within education categories, the age distributions of men and women are generally similar, although some differences in shape are visible, particularly in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups.

```{r}
sum(is.na(nhanes_data$MIMS))
```

```{r}
# Calculate total daily activity for each participant
total_activity =
  nhanes_data |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# Check participant-level total activity data
dim(total_activity)

total_activity |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Plot total activity against age by sex and education level
ggplot(
  total_activity,
  aes(
    x = age,
    y = total_activity,
    color = sex
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    method = "loess"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education Level",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total daily activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all education levels, although the pattern varies somewhat by group. The decline is most apparent among participants with less than a high school education. In the high school equivalent group, women tend to have higher total activity than men through much of middle age, while the difference becomes smaller at older ages. Among participants with more than a high school education, activity levels are relatively stable through early and middle adulthood but decline at older ages. Considerable individual variability is present within each group.

```{r}
# Calculate mean activity at each minute by sex and education level
activity_timecourse =
  nhanes_data |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_MIMS = mean(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Plot 24-hour activity time courses by sex and education level
ggplot(
  activity_timecourse,
  aes(
    x = minute,
    y = mean_MIMS,
    color = sex
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(
    se = FALSE,
    span = 0.08
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 360, 720, 1080, 1440),
    labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM", "12 AM")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Time of day",
    y = "Mean MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Across all education levels, activity follows a clear daily pattern: activity is lowest overnight, rises rapidly in the morning, remains relatively high throughout the day, and declines again in the evening. Sex differences are relatively small among participants with less than a high school education. In the high school equivalent and more than high school groups, women tend to have higher mean activity than men during much of the daytime, with the difference appearing most pronounced among participants with more than a high school education.


## Problem 3

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Import Citi Bike data and add year and month variables
jan_2020 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "January"
  )

jan_2024 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "January"
  )

july_2020 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2020,
    month = "July"
  )

july_2024 =
  read_csv("data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(
    year = 2024,
    month = "July"
  )
```

```{r}
# Combine all four Citi Bike datasets
citibike =
  bind_rows(
    jan_2020,
    july_2020,
    jan_2024,
    july_2024
  ) |>
  rename(
    weekday = weekdays
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(
      year,
      levels = c(2020, 2024)
    ),
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member"),
      labels = c("Casual", "Member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type),
    weekday = factor(
      weekday,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r}
# Check the cleaned Citi Bike dataset
dim(citibike)

citibike |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

```{r}
citibike |>
  select(
    ride_id,
    rideable_type,
    weekday,
    duration,
    start_station_name,
    end_station_name,
    member_casual,
    year,
    month
  ) |>
  glimpse()
```

```{r}
# Check ride duration
citibike |>
  summarize(
    min_duration = min(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_duration = max(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Check missing values
citibike |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ sum(is.na(.))
    )
  )
```

The cleaned Citi Bike dataset contains 99,485 rides and 9 variables. Each observation represents one ride and includes ride ID, bike type, day of the week, ride duration in minutes, starting and ending station names, membership status, year, and month. The data include rides from January and July in 2020 and 2024.

Ride duration ranges from approximately 1.0 to 238.8 minutes, with a median of about 9.8 minutes. Missing data are limited to station names: 43 rides are missing a starting station name and 207 are missing an ending station name. The remaining variables have no missing values.

```{r}
# Count rides by year, month, and membership status
ride_count_table =
  citibike |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  )

# Create a reader-friendly table
ride_count_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Casual", "Member"),
    caption = "Number of Citi Bike Rides by Year, Month, and Membership Status"
  )
```

Citi Bike members account for the majority of rides in every year-month combination. Ride volume is substantially higher in July than in January in both years, suggesting a strong seasonal pattern. Overall ridership is also higher in 2024 than in 2020, with the largest increase occurring in July. Casual ridership shows particularly strong seasonality, increasing sharply from January to July in both years.

```{r}
# Identify the 5 most popular starting stations in July 2024
top_stations =
  citibike |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(
    start_station_name,
    sort = TRUE
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

# Create a reader-friendly table
top_stations |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides"),
    caption = "Five Most Popular Citi Bike Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```

In July 2024, Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station among the sampled rides, followed by University Pl & E 14 St and W 21 St & 6 Ave.

```{r}
# Calculate median ride duration by year, month, and weekday
median_duration =
  citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekday) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# Plot median ride duration by weekday, month, and year
ggplot(
  median_duration,
  aes(
    x = weekday,
    y = median_duration,
    color = year,
    group = year
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the week",
    y = "Median ride duration (minutes)",
    color = "Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )
```

Median ride duration is generally longer in July than in January and is consistently higher in 2020 than in 2024. Weekend rides tend to have longer median durations than weekday rides, particularly in July. This weekend increase is especially pronounced in 2020, while the weekday pattern is flatter in January and more modest in 2024.

```{r}
# Keep 2024 Citi Bike rides
citibike_2024 =
  citibike |>
  filter(year == "2024")
```

```{r}
# Plot ride duration distributions by month, membership status, and bike type
ggplot(
  citibike_2024,
  aes(
    x = duration,
    fill = member_casual,
    color = member_casual
  )
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(
    rideable_type ~ month
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration Distribution in 2024",
    x = "Ride duration (minutes)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Membership status",
    color = "Membership status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Ride duration distributions in 2024 are strongly right-skewed across all groups, with most rides concentrated at shorter durations and a small number of much longer rides. Casual riders generally have longer and more variable ride durations than members, especially in July. Members show more concentrated distributions at shorter ride durations. Differences by bike type are present but appear smaller than the differences associated with membership status and month.
